reference.source: Kelley and Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology
clinicalPearls: Single-organ vasculitis denotes vasculitis confined to one organ or organ system without features of a systemic vasculitis, a category formalised in the current consensus nomenclature.

Recognised examples include isolated cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis, isolated aortitis, single-organ vasculitis of the gastrointestinal tract, testis, breast or urinary bladder, and isolated peripheral nerve vasculitis.
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring a thorough search for systemic disease before the 'single-organ' label is applied.
The distribution may be unifocal or multifocal within the affected organ, but by definition does not cross into other systems.
A subset of apparently localised disease later declares itself as systemic vasculitis, so ongoing surveillance is essential.
Histology (leukocytoclastic, granulomatous or necrotising) reflects the vessel size involved and helps frame differentials.
Management is often more conservative than systemic vasculitis; some cutaneous forms are self-limiting, while an isolated organ lesion such as focal aortitis may be treated surgically.
Isolated aortitis is frequently discovered incidentally in surgical aortic specimens and warrants assessment for large-vessel disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Single-organ vasculitis is inflammation of blood vessel walls restricted to a single organ or anatomical region, without the systemic distribution or serological markers of a defined systemic vasculitis. The vessel calibre involved varies by site and determines the histological pattern, ranging from leukocytoclastic small-vessel injury in isolated cutaneous disease to granulomatous or necrotising inflammation in isolated aortitis or nerve vasculitis. The initiating stimulus is usually unknown and may be immune-complex-mediated, cell-mediated or triggered by local factors. Because the same histology can be the first manifestation of a systemic process, single-organ vasculitis is defined partly by the absence of evidence for wider involvement over time.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic vasculitis with early or limited organ involvement
Vasculitis secondary to connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Tissue biopsy of the affected organ to characterise vessel size and inflammation
ANCA, ANA and complement to screen for systemic and autoimmune disease
Inflammatory markers and full systemic review of symptoms
Cross-sectional or vascular imaging appropriate to the organ involved
Screening for infective triggers including relevant serology
Age-appropriate malignancy screening where clinically indicated
Longitudinal follow-up to detect later systemic conversion
redFlags: Emergence of constitutional symptoms or new organ involvement suggesting systemic conversion
Aortic dilatation or dissection in isolated aortitis
Rapidly evolving mononeuropathy in isolated nerve vasculitis
Positive ANCA or other systemic serology on follow-up
reference.prognosis: Many single-organ forms have a favourable outlook, particularly self-limiting cutaneous disease, but prognosis depends on the organ affected and on whether the process later becomes systemic. Isolated aortitis and isolated nerve vasculitis carry organ-specific risks that require targeted follow-up.
pitfalls: Prematurely labelling disease as single-organ without excluding systemic vasculitis.
Failing to arrange follow-up, so later systemic conversion is missed.
Over-treating benign self-limiting cutaneous vasculitis with aggressive immunosuppression.
Overlooking incidental aortitis in surgical specimens and its implications for large-vessel disease.
Assuming a single negative serology permanently excludes systemic disease.
